arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Nichols' lawyer argued federal law did not apply to overseas moves before recently.
The government's lawyer argued the duty to update records is continuous.
Justice Roberts asked if the law leaves unregistration to states but not registration.
Justice Sotomayor questioned if the government used the wrong legal basis for extradition.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Nichols moved to the Philippines. He did not update his U.S. registration. The government charged him with a federal crime. Nichols claims federal law only applies when he returns. The government says the duty to update follows him.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Nichols wants the Court to rule that federal law does not apply while he is abroad.
The government wants the Court to rule that the duty to update registration persists overseas.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Nichols argues federal law only requires registration upon return to the United States.
The government argues the duty to keep registration current applies regardless of location.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the geographic reach of federal sex offender registration laws. It determines whether the government can prosecute offenders for failing to update records while living abroad. The outcome shapes federal enforcement power over citizens in foreign countries.
